hints: Picture the two curves on the same axes. At any given partial pressure of oxygen, is the right-hand curve higher or lower in % saturation?
Remember the golden rule: shift right means lower affinity. Does lower affinity mean haemoglobin holds on tighter, or lets go of oxygen more easily in respiring tissues?
walkthrough:
**Recall what the curve shows**

Think of the oxygen dissociation curve as a loading story. The x-axis is partial pressure of oxygen ($pO_2$), the y-axis is % saturation of haemoglobin.

High $pO_2$ (in lungs) means loading up, low $pO_2$ (in tissues) means unloading.

**Interpret a shift to the right**

A curve to the right sits lower at the same $pO_2$. That means for the same oxygen pressure, haemoglobin is less saturated.

Less saturated at the same pressure = lower affinity for oxygen, it does not hold on as tightly.

**Link to unloading in smaller mammals**

Lower affinity is very useful in tissues where $pO_2$ is low. Haemoglobin lets go of oxygen more readily, so more oxygen is released for respiration.

This makes perfect sense, as smaller mammals have a higher surface area to volume ratio and a faster metabolic rate, so they need quick unloading. That points to D.

options.A: At high $pO_2$ both curves approach 100% saturation. A right shift does not give extra carrying capacity, it changes affinity, not maximum load.
options.B: This is the opposite of a right shift. A right-shifted curve is less saturated at low $pO_2$, meaning it has already released oxygen more easily.
options.C: Saturating more easily means higher affinity, which is a shift to the left. A shift to the right means saturating less easily.
options.D: Right shift means lower affinity, so haemoglobin unloads (dissociates from) oxygen more easily at the low $pO_2$ found in respiring tissues.
